samples.L1: Maya rents, and she has saved $92,000: enough to put 20% down on a $400,000 home and pay the closing costs. Is her rent money wasted? We replay her choice from every month since 1991, one twin who buys and one who keeps renting, with real US home prices, rents and mortgage rates and every cost of owning: interest, property tax, insurance, repairs and the 6% it costs to sell. After ten years, how often did buying come out ahead, and when did it lose? History, not a forecast: no advice to buy or to rent.
samples.L2: Does renting really cost more than buying once you count the interest, the property tax, the insurance, the repairs and the cost of selling? We take two identical people with the same savings, one who buys a $400,000 home and one who rents a similar one, and replay them through 307 real start months since 1991, using real US home prices, rents and mortgage rates. The video shows how often the buyer was ahead after ten years, why buyers from 2006 fell behind, and how the answer moves with the rent you assume. History, not a forecast: no advice to buy or to rent.

roles.T: You are an American renter in 2026 with enough saved for a 20% down payment on a home near the national median price. You keep wondering whether paying rent is costing you more than buying would, once all the costs of owning are counted.
